case_studies.title: Harness-MU: A Safe, Governed, and Effective Harness for Multi-User LLM Agents
case_studies.abstract: The increasing deployment of large language model (LLM) agents in collaborative workflows demands robust multi-user, multi-principal interaction mechanisms capable of enforcing access permissions, resolving authoritative conflicts, and preventing unauthorized data disclosure. case_studies.title: RAVEN: Agentic RAG for Automated Vulnerability Repair
case_studies.abstract: Automated vulnerability repair has emerged as a promising direction to mitigate the growing number of software vulnerabilities. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have further accelerated research in automated repair. However, existing frameworks remain largely restricted to memory-related vulnerabilities and locally repairable vulnerability settings, leaving generalization to unseen vulnerability types underexplored. Their evaluations are often limited to a single programming language, and largely rely on proprietary models. In this paper, we propose RAVEN, a scalable, efficient
case_studies.summary: RAVEN is a system that automates the repair of software vulnerabilities, improving on existing frameworks by being more scalable and generalizable to different types of vulnerabilities. It was built using Large Language Models and can repair vulnerabilities in multiple programming languages. The result is a more efficient and effective way to mitigate software vulnerabilities.

case_studies.title: Agent-as-a-Router: Agentic Model Routing for Coding Tasks
case_studies.abstract: Real-world users typically have access to multiple Large Language Models (LLMs) from different providers, and these LLMs often excel at distinct domains, yet none dominate all. Consequently, routing each task to the most suitable model becomes critical for both performance and cost. Existing routers treat this as a static, one-off classification problem. However, we identify the performance bottleneck for these routers as information deficit: simply augmenting a vanilla LLM router with performance statistics at the task-dimension level yields a 15.3% relative gain, surpassing a heuristic route
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of routing coding tasks to the most suitable Large Language Model, by building a router that can dynamically choose the best model based on performance statistics, resulting in a 15.3% relative gain. They built an Agent-as-a-Router model that can make informed decisions about which model to use for a given task. This improves performance and reduces costs for users with access to multiple models.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure that uses Large Language Models, here is what to do: review your current routing setup, consider implementing a dynamic router that uses performance statistics, and evaluate the potential cost savings and performance gains. This flags a risk: if your org uses multiple LLMs, check your routing strategy immediately to ensure you're using the most suitable model for each task. Not directly applicable to general IT infrastructure work, but relevant to those who manage LLM deployments.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a novel routing mechanism for large language models. This is directly relevant to IT engineers working with LLM APIs, agentic systems, and MLOps.

case_studies.title: Capable but Careless: Do Computer-Use Agents Follow Contextual Integrity?
case_studies.abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) now act on a user's behalf across personal applications such as email, calendars, and to-do lists. This cross-application access is useful, but it also creates a privacy risk that has been largely overlooked: when an agent works in one context, it can pull in information from another that is inappropriate in that context. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of computer-use agents pulling in inappropriate information from other contexts, the authors built AgentCIBench to evaluate this risk, and the result is a way to identify and score potential failures. The research focuses on the privacy risks associated with cross-application access. It does not directly impact cloud infrastructure management.

case_studies.title: Training Open Models for Agentic Phone Use
case_studies.abstract: Phones are becoming an important execution surface for general-purpose agents, but training open models for reliable phone use remains difficult because the environment that matters at deployment, real devices running real apps, is slow, stateful, side-effectful, and hard to reset or verify, while scalable mock environments only approximate real behavior. We present PhoneBuddy, a training recipe and open-model line for agentic phone use that combines a real-app environment with a mock-app environment, PhoneWorld, which reconstructs runnable mock apps from real GUI usage structure. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of training open models for reliable phone use by creating PhoneBuddy, a training recipe that combines real-app and mock-app environments. The result is a more accurate and efficient way to train models for phone use. This research is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.

case_studies.title: AgentRiskBOM: A Risk-Scoping Security Bill of Materials for Agentic AI Systems
case_studies.abstract: Agentic AI systems retrieve private context, invoke tools, write files, call external services, coordinate with other agents, and may act without human approval. Existing bill of materials artifacts improve transparency for dependencies, model metadata, and training provenance, but leave an agentic transparency gap: capability opacity, the absence of a structured account of what a deployed agent can access, remember, change, delegate, and prove afterward. This paper introduces AgentRiskBOM, a security BOM for risk-scoping tool-using AI agents. It is an additive layer over SBOM, AIBOM, and MLBO
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of transparency gaps in agentic AI systems by introducing AgentRiskBOM, a security bill of materials that provides a structured account of what a deployed agent can access and do. The authors built AgentRiskBOM as an additive layer over existing bill of materials artifacts. The result is improved transparency and risk-scoping for AI systems.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI or machine learning systems, here is what to do: review your current bill of materials artifacts, consider implementing AgentRiskBOM to improve transparency and risk-scoping, and assess your systems for capability opacity risks.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a new concept of AgentRiskBOM, a security BOM for risk-scoping tool-using AI agents. It's an additive layer over existing BOMs and fills a specific gap in agentic transparency. This will likely resonate with IT engineers who work with AI systems and want to ensure the security of their agents. Although it might require more research and development, an IT engineer or consultant could potentially use this concept within 90 days to assess the security risks of deployed AI agents.

case_studies.title: Quantifying the Agreement Between Data-Influence and Data-Similarity to Understand LLM Behavior
case_studies.abstract: One way to understand LLM behavior is to trace its output back to the training data. Two types of measures are commonly used for output tracing: data-similarity and data-influence. The former is cheaper while the latter is believed to be more accurate. Even though many works have compared them for ground-truth tasks, no such comparisons exist for output tracing. Here, we fill this gap and precisely quantify the commonalities and differences between the two measures. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of understanding Large Language Model (LLM) behavior by comparing two measures, data-similarity and data-influence, to see how they agree on output tracing. The researchers built a system to quantify the commonalities and differences between these two measures. The result provides a better understanding of LLM behavior, but is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.

case_studies.title: Open Problem: Is AdamW Effective Under Heavy-Tailed Noise?
case_studies.abstract: AdamW is the de facto optimizer for training large language models (LLMs), yet the theory behind it still lives mostly in finite-variance regimes. This is increasingly unsatisfying, as empirical evidence indicates that stochastic gradient noise in LLM pretraining is typically heavy-tailed. Recent work shows that sign-based optimizers such as Lion and Muon achieve sharp heavy-tailed rates, and that AdaGrad can also converge under heavy-tailed noise. case_studies.summary: This research investigates the effectiveness of AdamW, a popular optimizer for training large language models, under heavy-tailed noise conditions. The authors aim to establish a rigorous convergence theory for AdamW in this regime. The result affects the training of large language models, but its direct impact on general cloud infrastructure management is unclear.

case_studies.title: Kamera: Unified Position-Invariant Multimodal KV Cache for Training-Free Reuse
case_studies.abstract: Multimodal agents repeatedly re-examine the same video frames, UI screenshots, and rendered artifacts as their context window slides and reasoning iterates, yet every look-back re-encodes from scratch, because prefix caches serve reuse only at a fixed leading position. We show this recompute is avoidable, and identify exactly what naive KV reuse loses: the cross-chunk conditioning a chunk absorbs from its neighbours. This loss is asymmetric. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of redundant computations in multimodal agents by introducing a unified position-invariant cache system, which allows for training-free reuse of previously computed results. The authors built a new type of cache called Kamera, which can recover the direct readout of a cached chunk exactly and for free. The result is a reduction in redundant computations, but it's not directly applicable to traditional IT infrastructure work.

case_studies.title: From RAN Control to Agentic Intelligence: Architecture and Vision for Energy Efficient AI-RAN
case_studies.abstract: Future 6G networks will rely on highly distributed, AI-native Radio Access Networks (RANs), where communication and AI workloads share a common infrastructure. This evolution, combined with increasing deployment density and continuous AI processing, is expected to significantly increase RAN energy consumption. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of increasing energy consumption in future 6G networks by introducing an architecture for energy-efficient AI-native Radio Access Networks.
